Nearby plots may have similar tree densities and species composition even
after accounting for canopy height. Soil, moisture, and management history
can vary across a forest without following stand boundaries. We extend the
[full plot-sampling model](full-model-plot-sampling.html) with spatial effects
that share information according to distance. Unlike the
[stratum example](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html), these effects vary
continuously across the forest rather than being shared within predefined groups.

We use a population with known spatial effects to examine parameter estimation,
map true and estimated relationships, and compare forest and stand
species-by-DBH densities with truth. The population uses the same forest,
151 plot locations, canopy heights, and 4,812 prediction cells as the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html), with new simulated counts.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the spatial-example data (ZIP)](downloads/spatial-plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="spatial-plot-sampling.zip"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
The archive includes the generated population, its true parameters and spatial
effects, and `generate_population.R` to reproduce it with seed 1.
The code below reads the supplied population; generating it again is optional.
:::

## Read the generated population

We read the plots, prediction cells, and generating parameters, along with
polygons for mapping and areas for stand summaries. Coordinates ending in
`_km` are in kilometers; the original coordinates and polygons are in meters.
The predictor `x` is canopy height standardized using the plots' mean and
standard deviation, as in the preceding articles.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

true_parameters <- read_csv("data/true_parameters.csv", na = "NA")

forest <- st_read("data/forest.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

prediction_cells <- st_read("data/prediction_cells.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

plot_locations <- st_read("data/plot_locations.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

cell_stand_areas <- read_csv("data/cell_stand_areas.csv")

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")
dbh_classes <- c("10-20", "20-30", "30-40", "40-50", "50+")
```

The CSV files include simulated counts for all 15 species-by-DBH categories.
Their `v` and `w` columns hold the true spatial effects, and three additional
columns hold the true combined intercepts. These provide comparisons after
fitting. We select only counts, areas, covariates, and coordinates when
constructing the model data below.

## Understand the generating model

### Spatial magnitude and species allocation

At location $\mathbf{s}_i$, expected tree density $M_i$ and the count $N_i$
on a plot of area $a_i$ hectares follow

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+v(\mathbf{s}_i),\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M).
$$

The zero-mean Gaussian process $v$ has covariance

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\{v(\mathbf{s}),v(\mathbf{s}')\}
=\sigma_v^2\exp\{-\phi_v\|\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}'\|\}.
$$

The spatial variance $\sigma_v^2$ determines variation on the log-density
scale. The decay $\phi_v$ controls how quickly correlation decreases with
distance; larger values describe shorter spatial dependence. We use
$\beta_0=\log(350)$, $\beta_1=-0.2$, $\sigma_v=0.5$, and $\phi_v=3$,
with negative-binomial size $r_M=1000$. At average canopy height and a zero
spatial effect, expected density is 350 trees/ha.

Species allocation proceeds through pine, then oak, with birch receiving
the remaining trees. At allocation step $j$, the conditional probability is

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi\{\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}x_i+\lambda_jw(\mathbf{s}_i)\},
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard Normal distribution function. The spatial
factor $w$ is independent of $v$, has mean zero and unit variance, and has
covariance $\exp\{-\phi_w\|\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}'\|\}$. Pine and oak share
this field, with loadings $\lambda_{\mathrm{pine}}=0.7$ and
$\lambda_{\mathrm{oak}}=-0.5$. A positive factor score increases pine's
allocation probability and decreases oak's probability among the remaining
trees. Pine is the anchor, so its loading is constrained to be positive.
The loadings determine the scale of the species effects because the factor
variance is fixed at one.

We use $\phi_w=5$. With distances in kilometers, the magnitude and composition
correlations fall to approximately 0.05 at 1 km and 0.6 km, respectively;
these effective spatial ranges are approximately $3/\phi$.
The species intercepts and canopy-height slopes, and all conditional DBH
regressions, match the earlier articles. No spatial effects or smoothing
are added to the DBH allocation models.

### Generate effects and counts together

We generate each spatial field jointly over the observed plots and prediction
cells. This connects both sets of locations to the same realized forest.
Each field is a full GP draw obtained from its covariance matrix using a
Cholesky factor. Given those fields, we draw total plot counts and allocate
them to species and then DBH classes.

The supplied files contain this completed population. The optional code below
shows the construction; the downloadable script includes the conditional DBH
allocation and writes the resulting files. Running `source("generate_population.R")`
reproduces the supplied population. Full-GP generation requires substantially
more memory than reading these files.

## Fit with nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes

We fit nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes (NNGPs), which approximate the
full GP through conditional distributions involving a small set of nearby
locations [@datta2016nngp]. This avoids factoring a covariance matrix for
all prediction cells. We use 15 neighbors for both spatial terms.

We first arrange counts into one row per plot, species, and DBH class.

```{r}
#| label: model-data

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, easting_km, northing_km, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  ) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species, dbh_class)

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, design = fixedArea(area)
)
```

`nngp()` adds the magnitude spatial effect. `factor_nngp()` adds one spatial
species factor, with `anchors = "pine"` identifying its positive loading.
Both spatial decays, the magnitude variance, and the species loadings are
estimated using automatic starting values and default priors.

```{r}
#| label: fit

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x + nngp(easting_km, northing_km, m = 15, name = "space"),
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x + factor_nngp(easting_km, northing_km, K = 1, m = 15,
                              anchors = "pine", name = "space"),
    dbh_class | species ~ x
  ),
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 6000,
    n_burn = 2000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    nb_size = 1000,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

Each chain contributes 4,000 retained draws after discarding 2,000 burn-in
iterations. The chains run on separate cores where supported. Negative-binomial
size is fixed at its generating value, as in the stratum example; magComp
does not estimate size alongside magnitude random effects.

## Compare parameters and check the chains

We add the generating values to the parameter summary. This table focuses
on the magnitude and species models; `summary(fit)` also includes the DBH
regression coefficients. The variance, decay, and loading rows describe the
spatial covariance structure.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-summary

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

main_parameters <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(component == "magnitude" | block == "species") |>
  left_join(true_parameters, by = c("component", "block", "parameter", "index"))

main_parameters |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

The intervals for the magnitude variance, both spatial decays, and the
species loadings include their generating values. The composition decay
has a broad interval, indicating uncertainty about its spatial range.
A single realized forest and its sampled plots need not identify the
covariance parameters precisely.

The magnitude intercept has an R-hat of about 1.07 and an ESS of 27;
the other parameters in this table have R-hats below 1.05. An intercept and its
spatial effect can trade off: increasing $\beta_0$ and lowering $v$ can
leave $\beta_0+v(\mathbf{s})$ almost unchanged. We therefore also inspect
combined intercepts, as in the stratum article. For species, these are
$\alpha_{0j}+\lambda_jw(\mathbf{s})$.

We use all retained draws to assess the combined intercepts averaged over
the observed plot locations.

```{r}
#| label: combined-diagnostics

diagnostics <- samples(fit, type = "combined", group = ".all")

summary(diagnostics) |>
  transmute(quantity = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude",
                                paste(str_to_title(stick), "allocation")),
            rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Quantity", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

These combined intercepts have R-hats near one and much larger effective
sample sizes. Their improved diagnostics describe the sums, without changing
the separate intercept's diagnostic. `plot(diagnostics)` can be used to
inspect their chains.

## Predict jointly across the forest

For each retained parameter draw, `predict()` generates spatial effects at
new locations conditional on observed effects and previously generated
prediction effects. We supply the complete prediction grid in one call so
forest and stand summaries retain this joint spatial variation.

The observation target then generates total counts and species-by-DBH
allocations. We retain 100 draws per chain for prediction and divide counts
by their cell areas through `type = "density"`. Setting `keep_effects = TRUE`
also keeps the latent draws used in these same predictions for mapping.

```{r}
#| label: predict

set.seed(1)

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, stand_id, x, area, easting_km, northing_km),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples",
  keep_effects = TRUE
)
```

### Map true and estimated combined intercepts

We extract the combined intercepts at prediction locations and join them to
the true values. `samples()` uses the stored draws; it does not simulate a
second set of spatial effects. The magnitude combined intercept is log
density at average canopy height. Species combined intercepts are on the
probit scale at that same canopy height.

```{r}
#| label: map-values

intercept_summary <- summary(samples(predictions, type = "combined")) |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit),
         component = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude",
                              str_to_title(stick)))

true_intercepts <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, magnitude_intercept, pine_intercept, oak_intercept) |>
  pivot_longer(-plot_id, names_to = "component", values_to = "truth") |>
  mutate(component = recode(component, magnitude_intercept = "Magnitude",
                             pine_intercept = "Pine", oak_intercept = "Oak"))

map_values <- intercept_summary |>
  select(plot_id, component, Estimate = mean) |>
  left_join(true_intercepts, by = c("plot_id", "component")) |>
  rename(Truth = truth) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Truth, Estimate), names_to = "source", values_to = "intercept") |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, levels = c("Magnitude", "Pine", "Oak")),
         source = factor(source, levels = c("Truth", "Estimate")))

intercept_maps <- prediction_cells |>
  left_join(map_values, by = "plot_id",
             relationship = "many-to-many")
```

Truth and posterior means share a color scale within each figure. White
circles mark the sampled plots. These maps compare combined intercepts;
variation due to canopy height enters separately when calculating densities
and allocation probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: fig-magnitude-intercepts
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined magnitude intercepts on the log-density scale. White circles show sampled plot locations."

ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component == "Magnitude")) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_locations, shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 0.7,
          stroke = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ source, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept\n(log-density)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-species-intercepts
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined species allocation intercepts on a common probit scale. Oak allocation is conditional on a tree not being pine."

ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component %in% c("Pine", "Oak"))) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_locations, shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 0.7,
          stroke = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(component ~ source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept\n(probit)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

The estimates show the broad spatial patterns, with less local variation
than truth between sampled plots. The maps show posterior means; prediction
and area summaries also retain uncertainty about the spatial effects.

## Compare forest densities with truth

We pass the predictive density draws to `standSummary()`, using cell areas
as weights. The returned samples contain one forest density for each
species-by-DBH category in every draw. Their means and 95% posterior
predictive intervals can be compared with the realized simulated counts
per unit area.

```{r}
#| label: forest-summary

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(prediction$area), .groups = "drop")

forest_comparison <- forest_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = "category") |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black horizontal marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(forest_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The forest summaries combine spatially varying magnitude and species
allocation with canopy height and conditional DBH allocation. Their
uncertainty includes parameter uncertainty, jointly predicted spatial
effects, and count variation.

## Compare stand densities with truth

The prepared area table identifies each cell's area within each stand.
A cell that crosses stand boundaries contributes the same density draw to
each stand, weighted by its overlap area. We use that table for both the
predictions and simulated truth, following the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html#cell-areas-within-stands).

```{r}
#| label: stand-summary

stand_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = cell_stand_areas,
  unit = prediction_id,
  group = stand_id,
  represented_area = area_ha,
  summary = "samples"
)

stand_truth <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  inner_join(cell_stand_areas, by = c("plot_id" = "prediction_id"),
              relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(stand_id, category) |>
  summarise(truth = weighted.mean(count / area, area_ha), .groups = "drop")

stand_comparison <- summary(stand_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(stand_id = unit) |>
  left_join(stand_truth, by = c("stand_id", "category")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order))
```

Each point below represents one species-by-DBH density in one of the 249
stands. The axes have matching limits within each species panel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stand-densities
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true species-by-DBH densities across all stands. Faint bars show 95% posterior predictive intervals; dashed lines mark equality."

stand_limits <- stand_comparison |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(limit = max(truth, mean, q97_5), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(stand_comparison, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_blank(data = stand_limits, aes(x = limit, y = limit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "True density (trees/ha)", y = "Estimated density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

Spatial effects allow information from nearby sampled plots to inform
predictions within each stand. Stand boundaries determine the areas over
which we summarize predictions; they do not constrain the spatial processes.
The same joint prediction draws support both forest and stand summaries.

The [conditional DBH-effects article](conditional-dbh-effects-plot-sampling.html)
adds a spatial factor to size allocation within species. It explains how a
shared factor can affect different species and DBH allocation steps through
their own loadings, and briefly shows a stratum alternative.

For repeated inventories, the [space-time article](space-time-effects-plot-sampling.html)
extends the magnitude and species effects to describe dependence across
both locations and measurement years.
